description: Finding patterns in th earth and solving their problems
summary: ThermoTrace is a web app built for the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge. It uses 25 years of NASA POWER data (2001–2025) to answer four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users pick one of six regions (Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, Cairo, Delhi or Phoenix) and a variable (land surface temperature, daytime or night-time air temperature, average air temperature, or precipitation). The app plots the yearly values, measures the rate of change with Sen’s slope, tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test, and explains the result in plain language. It also compares urban and non-urban sites, all six regions, and day versus night. Our findings: surface temperature rose significantly in five regions (0.24 to 0.47 °C per decade) but fell in Delhi (0.38 °C per decade), showing that the same variable can trend in opposite directions in different places. Night-time temperatures are warming significantly in five of the six regions, while daytime temperatures are warming in only three. By making NASA data easy to explore and honest about significance, ThermoTrace can support urban planning, climate adaptation and education.
details:
ThermoTrace is a web app that helps people explore how Earth’s climate is changing, using NASA data. It was built for the “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” challenge and answers its four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

How it works. Users choose one of six regions (Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, Cairo, Delhi or Phoenix) and a variable: land surface temperature, daytime air temperature, night-time air temperature, average air temperature or precipitation. The app shows 25 years of annual values (2001–2025) on an interactive chart for an urban site and a nearby non-urban site. It measures the rate of change with Sen’s slope, tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test, and writes the result in plain language. It also compares all six regions side by side and compares day with night. Users can upload their own data as a CSV file.

What we found. Surface temperature rose significantly in five regions (0.24 to 0.47 °C per decade) but fell in Delhi (0.38 °C per decade). Night-time temperatures are warming significantly in five of the six regions, while daytime temperatures are warming in only three.

Benefits and impact. Users do not have to work through large datasets themselves. ThermoTrace makes NASA data easier to understand and shows clearly when a trend is real and when it is not. We hope it can support education, research, urban planning and climate adaptation.

Tools. The app is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no external libraries. The data come from NASA POWER, which is based on NASA’s MERRA-2 reanalysis. We used AI tools (Claude) to generate the code and text, and Gamma to prepare the presentation.

What makes it creative. ThermoTrace brings data exploration, comparison across places, day-versus-night analysis and statistical testing together in one place, and it turns the statistics into a plain-language case summary.

What we considered. We considered the difference between land surface temperature and air temperature, how to compare urban and non-urban sites fairly, and the limits of the data. NASA POWER grid cells are about 50 km wide, so the app shows regional trends, not the heat of individual neighbourhoods. Our next step is to add 1 km NASA MODIS data for street-level analysis.
